slides.title: What Are Git and GitHub?
slides.html:
Slide 02 / 23 CORE ARCHITECTURE

Git vs. GitHub: The Tool vs. The Platform

Understanding the clear boundary between the local version control engine and the cloud hub.

Git (The Local Engine)

Local Software

A version control system installed on your machine. Tracks exact file revisions, branches, and commits offline in the hidden .git/ directory.

• Runs 100% Offline • Instant Branching • Cryptographic Integrity

GitHub (The Cloud Platform)

Cloud Service

A cloud hosting platform for Git repositories. Enables global team collaboration, code reviews, Pull Requests, issues, and automated CI/CD deployments.

• Remote Backups • Pull Requests (PR) • CI/CD Automation
💡 Key takeaway: You can use Git offline without GitHub, but you use GitHub to share Git repositories.
The Connection: Local Computer (Git) ➔ Cloud Remote (GitHub) Flow Diagram

slides.title: Why Do We Need Git?
slides.html:
Slide 03 / 23 THE PROBLEM & SOLUTION

Why Every Software Engineer Uses Git

Eliminating the nightmare of lost code, zip duplicates, and blind overwrites.

✕ The Old Nightmare (Without Git)

CHAOS
📁 desktop/my-project/
├── 📦 project-final.zip
├── 📦 project-final2.zip
├── 📦 project-final-REAL.zip
└── 📦 project-final-REAL-v2-final.zip (which one works?)
  • ✗ Accidentally deleting working code with no undo
  • ✗ Two teammates overwriting each other's files
  • ✗ Zero audit trail of who broke production or when

✓ The Modern Solution (With Git)

CONFIDENCE
📁 my-project/
├── 📁 .git/ (entire infinite history stored here)
├── 📄 src/index.js
└── 📄 README.md (clean, single folder, no zip copies)
  • ✓ Time Machine: Jump to any commit in your project history
  • ✓ Safe Sandbox: Branch off and experiment without risking main
  • ✓ Full Accountability: Every line has author and reason stamped

slides.title: The 4 Core Git Areas
slides.html:
Slide 04 / 23 CORE ARCHITECTURE

The 4 Essential Git Areas

How your code moves between your working disk, staging index, commit history, and GitHub.

The Complete Lifecycle: Working Directory ➔ Staging Area ➔ Local Repo ➔ Remote Repo Core Diagram
1
Working Directory
Your actual files on disk that you edit in VS Code. Changes are untracked or modified.
2
Staging Area (Index) git add
The preparation lounge. You curate exactly which file changes will be included in the next snapshot.
3
Local Repository git commit
Your local database inside .git/ storing permanent commit snapshots with cryptographic hashes.
4
Remote Repository (GitHub) git push
The cloud copy hosted on GitHub for team collaboration, code reviews, and remote backups.

slides.title: Check if Git Is Installed
slides.html:
Slide 05 / 23 STEP 1: INSTALLATION

Check if Git Is Installed

Verifying your terminal environment before beginning your developer workflow.

Terminal — Shell Verification
$ git --version
git version 2.45.2
# If installed, Git prints its active version string.
✓
If a version string like git version 2.x.x is printed, Git is successfully configured on your system!

What if Git is not installed?

If you get command not found: git, install it for your OS in 30 seconds:

macOS: xcode-select --install
Windows: git-scm.com (Git Bash)
Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install git
Tip: Git Bash is the recommended command terminal for Windows developers.

slides.title: Basic Git Configuration
slides.html:
Slide 06 / 6 STEP 2: SETUP IDENTITY

Configure Your Developer Identity

Git stamps your name and email onto every commit snapshot you create.

Terminal — Global Identity Setup
$ git config --global user.name "Alice Chen"
$ git config --global user.email "alice@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main
$ git config --global --list
user.name=Alice Chen
user.email=alice@example.com
init.defaultBranch=main
⚙️ The --global flag configures these settings for every repository on your machine.

Why Does Git Need Your Email?

GitHub matches the commit author email to your GitHub profile. This ensures your commits earn green contribution squares on your profile graph!

Live GitHub Commit Badge Preview:
AC
Alice Chen Verified ✓ alice@example.com • 2 mins ago
Note: Git local identity is purely metadata, not your GitHub login password.

slides.title: Create a New Project
slides.html:
Slide 07 / 23 STEP 3: WORKSPACE SETUP

Create Your Project Directory

Setting up a clean folder structure before initializing version control.

Terminal — Create Project Workspace
$ mkdir my-website
$ cd my-website
$ echo "# My Awesome Website" > README.md
$ echo "<h1>Hello World</h1>" > index.html
$ ls -la
total 8
-rw-r--r-- 1 user staff 21 README.md
-rw-r--r-- 1 user staff 23 index.html
📁 We now have a project folder with 2 files, but Git is not tracking it yet!

Folder Tree State

📁 my-website/
├── 📄 README.md (Documentation)
└── 📄 index.html (Web page)
⚠️ Notice: At this moment, this is an ordinary folder. If you edit or delete files, there is no undo or history until we initialize Git in the next step.

slides.title: Initialize Git
slides.html:
Slide 08 / 23 STEP 4: INITIALIZE REPO

Initialize Git with git init

Transforming a plain folder into an intelligent, version-controlled repository.

Terminal — git init
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /my-website/.git/
# Notice your terminal prompt now shows branch '(main)'!
Golden Rule: NEVER delete or manually edit the .git folder! That hidden folder contains your repository's entire history and commit timeline.
What git init creates: HEAD pointer, repository config, and object database. Internal Structure

slides.title: git status
slides.html:
Slide 09 / 23 STEP 5: THE COMPASS

Check Status with git status

Your most vital diagnostic command — run git status whenever you are unsure.

Terminal — git status diagnostic
$ git status
On branch main
No commits yet
Untracked files:
(use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
README.md
index.html
nothing added to commit but untracked files present
RED Files listed in red are Untracked: Git sees them on disk, but they are not yet part of your commit snapshot.
Traffic Light: Untracked (Red) ➔ Staged (Green) ➔ Committed (Blue) Lifecycle States

slides.title: git add
slides.html:
Slide 10 / 23 STEP 6: STAGING AREA

Stage Files with git add

Selecting and queuing specific file changes for the upcoming snapshot.

Terminal — Staging files
$ git add README.md index.html
$ git status
On branch main
No commits yet
Changes to be committed:
(use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
new file: README.md
new file: index.html
GREEN Files now turned GREEN! They are safely staged in the index, ready for the commit snapshot.

3 Ways to Stage Changes

git add index.html Stages only the specified single file. Safest and most precise.
git add . Stages all new, modified, and deleted files in the current folder.
git add -A Stages all changes across the entire repository root.
Pro Tip: Only stage files that belong to the same logical feature or bug fix.

slides.title: Check the Staged Changes
slides.html:
Slide 11 / 23 STEP 7: DIFF INSPECTION

Inspect Line Diffs Before Committing

Reviewing exactly what lines were added, modified, or deleted.

Terminal — git diff --staged
$ git diff --staged
diff --git a/index.html b/index.html
--- /dev/null
+++ b/index.html
@@ -0,0 +1,5 @@
+<!DOCTYPE html>
+<html>
+ <body>
+ <h1>My Awesome Website</h1>
+ </body>
+</html>
🔍 + indicates added lines, while - indicates removed lines.

Essential Diff Commands

git diff

Compares Working Directory changes that have NOT yet been staged.

git diff --staged

Compares files currently in Staging against your last commit.

git restore --staged <file>

Unstages a file without losing any of your written code.

Senior habit: Always review your diffs before committing!

slides.title: Create Your First Commit
slides.html:
Slide 12 / 23 STEP 8: PERMANENT SNAPSHOT

Save Permanent Snapshots with git commit

Freezing your staged changes forever into Git history with a cryptographic hash.

Terminal — git commit -m
$ git commit -m "feat: initial commit with README and index"
[main (root-commit) 4f8a12c] feat: initial commit with README and index
2 files changed, 7 insertions(+)
create mode 100644 README.md
create mode 100644 index.html
📸 Anatomy of a Great Commit Message: • feat: new user feature  |  fix: bug patch  |  docs: markdown update Always write in imperative present tense ("Add login form", not "Added").
Each commit is a snapshot pointing to parent commit, author, timestamp, and SHA hash. Snapshot Model

slides.title: View Commit History
slides.html:
Slide 13 / 23 STEP 9: THE TIMELINE

Explore History with git log

Navigating your project's commit timeline and visual commit graph.

Terminal — git log --oneline --graph
$ git log --oneline --graph --decorate
* 9b4d1a2 (HEAD -> main) feat: add user authentication API
* 5c2e8f1 feat: add responsive navigation bar
* 4f8a12c feat: initial commit with README and index
📍 HEAD is the bookmark pointer that indicates which branch and commit you are currently working on.
Understanding Git CLI syntax: Core Tool, Action Verb, Flag/Option, and Arguments. CLI Anatomy

slides.title: What Is a Branch?
slides.html:
Slide 14 / 23 STEP 10: ISOLATED WORKSPACES

Isolate Features with Git Branches

Developing new features in parallel without ever breaking the main production branch.

Why Branching Is Magic in Git

In Git, a branch is merely a 41-byte pointer to a commit hash. Creating a branch is virtually instantaneous (0.001s) and takes zero extra disk space.

🌿 Branch Naming Conventions:
• feature/user-login (New user capabilities) • fix/checkout-button (Bug patches) • docs/api-guide (Documentation updates)
🛡️ Golden Rule: The main branch must always be stable and deployable.
Visual Flow: feature/login branching from main, independent commits, and merging back into C5. Branch Model

slides.title: Create and Switch Branch
slides.html:
Slide 15 / 23 STEP 11: BRANCH MANAGEMENT

Modern Branch Commands: switch & merge

Creating, switching, merging, and deleting feature branches.

Terminal — Modern Branch Workflow
$ git switch -c feature/navbar
Switched to a new branch 'feature/navbar'
$ git commit -am "feat: add navigation component"
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git merge feature/navbar
Fast-forward  |  1 file changed, 12 insertions(+)
⚡ git switch is the modern syntax introduced in Git 2.23 (cleaner than legacy git checkout).

Branch Command Cheat Card

git branch

List all local branches (* marks current active branch).

git switch -c <branch>

Create a new branch and immediately switch into it.

git merge <branch>

Integrates changes from target branch into current branch.

git branch -d <branch>

Safely deletes branch once merged.

slides.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
slides.html:
Slide 16 / 23 STEP 12: CONFLICT RESOLUTION

Resolving Merge Conflicts Like a Pro

What happens when two branches touch the exact same lines, and how to fix it cleanly.

Don't Panic: Conflicts Are Normal

When two branches modify the same line, Git stops and asks the human developer to decide which version to keep.

4-Step Resolution Recipe:
1. Open the file in VS Code 2. Click Accept Current or Accept Incoming 3. Remove markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) 4. Run git add . & git commit to finish!
VS Code highlights conflicts with quick one-click resolution buttons!
Visual Conflict Editor: Accept Current Change (HEAD) vs Accept Incoming Change (feature) Conflict Editor

slides.title: Connect Local Repo to GitHub
slides.html:
Slide 17 / 23 STEP 13: CLOUD CONNECTION

Connect Your Local Repo to GitHub

Creating a remote repository on GitHub and linking it via origin URL.

Terminal — Link Remote Origin
$ git remote add origin https://github.com/user/my-website.git
$ git branch -M main
$ git remote -v
origin https://github.com/user/my-website.git (fetch)
origin https://github.com/user/my-website.git (push)
🌐 origin is the standard nickname Git uses to refer to your main remote cloud repository URL.
Step 1: Create an empty repository on GitHub without README (we already have local files). GitHub UI

slides.title: Push and Pull with GitHub
slides.html:
Slide 18 / 23 STEP 14: CLOUD SYNC

Push & Pull with GitHub Cloud

Uploading your local commits to GitHub and pulling updates down from teammates.

Terminal — git push -u origin main
$ git push -u origin main
Enumerating objects: 6, done.
Writing objects: 100% (6/6), 540 bytes, done.
To https://github.com/user/my-website.git
* [new branch] main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
Next pushes become super simple: Because -u sets up upstream tracking, you can now simply run git push and git pull!
Your project is now live on GitHub with complete commit history, branches, and code view! Repository View

slides.title: What Is .gitignore?
slides.html:
Slide 19 / 23 STEP 15: SECURITY & HYGIENE

Protect Secrets & Cleanliness with .gitignore

Telling Git which files and folders must NEVER be tracked or pushed to the cloud.

What MUST Be in .gitignore:

🔒 .env (API Keys, DB Passwords) 📁 node_modules/ (Downloaded dependencies) 📁 dist/ & build/ (Generated files) 📄 .DS_Store (OS metadata junk)
🚨 Critical Security Warning: Never push credentials or .env to GitHub. Automated bot scanners inspect public repositories in under 3 seconds!
Green Shield: Tracked Source Code (.js, .html) vs Red Lock: Ignored (.env, node_modules) Security & Hygiene

slides.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
slides.html:
Slide 21 / 23 STEP 17: THE SAFETY NET

How to Undo in Git: Emergency Guide

Four everyday mistakes and the exact terminal commands to recover safely.

The Safety Net: In Working Directory (restore) ➔ In Staging (restore --staged) ➔ Committed (revert/amend) Emergency Safety Net
1. "I broke a file, take me back to last commit!" git restore <file>
Discards unstaged modifications in the working tree.
2. "I staged a file by accident!" git restore --staged <file>
Unstages the file back to working tree without deleting code.
3. "Typo in last commit message!" git commit --amend -m "..."
Rewrites the most recent commit message smoothly.
4. "Need to switch branches but work unfinished!" git stash
Shelves changes safely; restore later with git stash pop.

slides.title: Hands-on Exercise
slides.html:
Slide 22 / 23 STEP 18: STUDENT LAB

Hands-on Mission: Your First Git Project

Put your knowledge into practice with this end-to-end terminal exercise drill.

Student Mission Checklist

Complete these 6 steps in your terminal to earn your Git badge:

1 Create & initialize repository
2 Stage & commit initial index.html
3 Create branch feature/styles
4 Add styles.css & commit on branch
5 Switch to main & merge feature
6 Push to GitHub with git push
🎉 All commands can be copied directly from the terminal block!
Terminal — Student Challenge Drill
$ mkdir portfolio && cd portfolio
$ git init
$ echo "<h1>My Portfolio</h1>" > index.html
$ git add . && git commit -m "feat: initial portfolio"
$ git switch -c feature/styles
$ echo "body { background: #0f172a; color: #fff; }" > styles.css
$ git add . && git commit -m "style: dark theme styles"
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature/styles
$ git log --oneline --graph
# Mission Accomplished! 🚀

slides.title: Questions & Wrap Up
slides.html:
Slide 23 / 23 GRADUATION

Congratulations! You Have Mastered Git

Review the golden rules of professional software development and version control.

The 4 Golden Rules of Version Control

1. Atomic Commits Make small, frequent commits for one purpose at a time.
2. Meaningful Messages Explain why the change was made in clear imperative sentences.
3. Pull Before Push Always sync remote changes to avoid merge conflicts.
4. Branch for Features Never commit broken experiments directly into main.
